newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dollar shows baht positive side of float.
newsitem.headline: Australia dollar shows baht positive side of float.

text.p: As the Thai baht contemplates life under a floating regime, the experience of the Australian dollar shows that while wild swings are inevitable, volatility does recede with time.

And analysts argue that in the 14 years since the dollar was set free, it has added a discipline to economic decision-making which has discouraged profligate policies and forced Australia to address its national savings imbalance.
"You would be hard-pressed to find an economist to say the experience of floating has not been a good one for Australia," said John Kyriakopoulos, a senior economist at J.P. Morgan.
The dollar's early experience after financial deregulation in December 1983 was not a happy one as it crumbled from over 94 U.S. cents to under 65 cents in little more than a year.
But neither had the managed regime prevented poor fundamentals from making themselves felt -- at the start of 1982, for instance, the dollar had been worth US$1.10.

The nadir was reached in 1986 when a ballooning budget deficit, labour market strife, rampant inflation and, above all, an explosion in Australia's current account deficit led to a now infamous outburst from the then Treasurer Paul Keating.
In an off-the-cuff remark he warned Australia was at risk of becoming a "banana republic" if its trade deficit was not dealt with.
Offshore investors, alarmed by such candour, dumped the dollar in a wild selling spree which saw it reach an all-time low around 59 cents in July that year.
But economists reckoned the crisis proved cathartic in the end in that it forced the government to take the tough economic decisions which were needed.
"A floating rate is a constraint on pursuing policies which are not sound," said Kyrikopoulos. "In some ways the market was acting as a policeman -- and it worked."

Once the government began to deal with the fundamental problems of the country the dollar steadily appreciated and for the last 10 year has basically fluctuated around a flat trend. That has corresponded to about 56.5 on its trade weighted index and around 75 cents against the U.S. currency.
"If you get the fundamentals right the currency will come round to its natural level," said Bruce Freeland, chief economist at Commonwealth Bank.
"And freeing the exchange rate allowed policy to concentrate on getting domestic policy right -- the government has not had to set levers just to keep the dollar at a particular level."
In this regard Freeland felt the adventures of sterling in the European Monetary System in 1993 was most instructive for the Thai authorities in the new floating era.
"The experience proved beyond doubt that using interest rates to keep a currency at levels inconsistent with domestic fundamentals just makes you vulnerable to speculators," he said.

The U.K. government raised rates to 15 percent from 10 percent in a last ditch attempt to keep the pound in the system but the market knew full well it was unsustainable with the economy already well into recession.
Within a matter of hours after the hike, the pound was free.
The U.K. slashed rates in the months afterwards and so began an economic recovery which is the envy of Europe.
This was why the decision of the Thai authorities to raise interest rates today seemed so perverse, said Freeland.
The Bank of Thailand raised its key bank rate to 12.5 percent from 10.5 percent.

"Allowing the float is great news for Thailand but the desire to "manage" it is self-defeating," he said. "The last thing the economy and the banking system there needs is a higher cost for money -- such rates are simply not sustainable."
